articles.title: Brady Tkachuk gets ice-cold reception in return to Ottawa with Florida Panthers
articles.summary: OTTAWA, Ontario (AP) — A regular-season game in October wouldn’t normally attract much attention for the Ottawa Senators.Former captain Brady Tkachuk was boo...
articles.body:
OTTAWA, Ontario (AP) — A regular-season game in October wouldn't normally attract much attention for the Ottawa Senators. But this one was different.

Former captain Brady Tkachuk was booed loudly in his return to Ottawa with the Florida Panthers, four months after requesting a trade from the only NHL team he'd ever known.

Fans drowned out a video tribute to Tkachuk with profane chants during Ottawa's 5-1 victory Wednesday night. The star forward opened the scoring with a power-play goal midway through the first period, but that was all the offense Florida could muster.

Tkachuk seemed to revel in the hostile atmosphere. He raised his stick in acknowledgment during the tribute and waved at fans with his trademark grin.

Drafted fourth overall in 2018, Tkachuk spent eight seasons with the Senators. A fan favorite for much of his tenure, he helped Ottawa return to the playoffs in 2025, ending a seven-year drought.

His relationship with some fans grew strained last season, though. Tkachuk and his brother, Matthew, a star winger for the Panthers, faced criticism over their "Wingmen" podcast, while Brady's decision to attend a White House celebration following the U.S. men's Olympic gold medal also drew backlash.

Speculation about Tkachuk's future in Ottawa intensified late last season. At the team's season-ending news conference in April, he acknowledged the rumors had become a distraction, insisting, "I have been fully committed to this team."

Less than two months later, Tkachuk was traded to Florida, where his brother has won two Stanley Cup championships.

"I've talked about it a lot that, you know, there's professional reasons, personal reasons why I wasn't going to re-sign here, and a lot of those things have remained private between (Senators GM Steve Staios) and I," Tkachuk said.

"It's going to remain private. It just happened to work out this way."

Senators owner Michael Andlauer previously suggested Tkachuk's father, Keith, and brother Matthew influenced his decision to request a trade.

"Yeah, I saw the quote and he's entitled to his opinion," Tkachuk said. "I know for myself it was 100% my decision. I can make decisions for myself and my family."

Tkachuk had dinner with several former teammates Tuesday night, but Tim Stutzle wasn't among them.

"I haven't seen him," Stutzle said. "I have a chef at home, so I didn't go for dinner."

A number of fans altered their Tkachuk jerseys to express their displeasure. Season-ticket holder Neil Kennelly and his son Nolan both wore Tkachuk jerseys with an X taped over the captain's C.

On the back, Nolan had covered Tkachuk's name with the words "Wingmen is trash."

"I'm not going to say I was crazy angry or surprised, but you know what? He doesn't want to be here, don't let the door hit you on the way out," Neil Kennelly said. "We want people who want to be here."

A group of four friends had similar perspectives. All four had Tkachuk jerseys and had changed the name plate.

"He says he's a big boy, but his brother and dad made the decision for him," said Phil Grant.

Tkachuk got off to a slow start this season but entered the game as the NHL's first star of the week after scoring natural hat tricks in back-to-back games.

Tkachuk said he arrived at the rink around 8:30 a.m. and was happy to reconnect with staff members and others he had grown close to during his eight seasons in Ottawa.

The 27-year-old admitted he hadn't given much thought to how emotional his return might be, but he was looking forward to seeing the fans who supported him and his family during his time in the nation's capital.

"I've had so many great memories here that will last forever," Tkachuk said before the game. "And I don't know what the exact emotion is going to be, but I just know how thankful and appreciative I am for everything that's happened the last eight years."

Fans cheered when Artem Zub checked Tkachuk on his first shift and he went down. There was a playoff atmosphere in the building, with fans chanting "We don't need you!" and "Matthew's better!" and "You betrayed us!"

Tkachuk said it had been difficult to hear and read speculation surrounding his departure, but added he knew he gave his all in Ottawa and that any negative reaction from fans wouldn't change how he felt about the city.

"I know how I feel about this city, about this fan base, and I'm thankful and appreciative," he said. "And no matter what the reaction's going to be, it's not going to change how I feel about this city and this fan base."

Senators fans have endured their share of messy departures over the years, from former captain Alexei Yashin to Dany Heatley's trade request and the eventual exits of captains Jason Spezza and Erik Karlsson.

But none returned to Ottawa under circumstances quite as acrimonious as Tkachuk.

articles.title: Brady Tkachuk gets mercilessly booed by Senators fans during return to Ottawa
articles.summary: Senators fans unleash brutal chants at Brady Tkachuk during his emotional return.
articles.body:
Brady Tkachuk received a hostile welcome during his return to Ottawa on Wednesday night. The former Ottawa Senators captain faced loud boos and insulting chants as the Florida Panthers visited the Canadian Tire Centre.

NHL reporter Claire Hanna shared footage of Tkachuk's tribute video on X.

"A video tribute to former Ottawa Captain Brady Tkachuk was just played during the TV timeout at the Canadian Tire Centre," Hanna wrote. "Brady salutes the crowd with a big smile while the crowd shares their displeasure."

Hanna also revealed several chants directed at Tkachuk throughout the game. Fans shouted "We don't need you," "Traitor," and "You're a sellout."

Other chants included personal insults and a pointed message about his podcast, like "Who's your daddy?" "You eat crayons," "You're a sellout," and "You can't read."

Brady Tkachuk's return ends in Ottawa's win

The reception followed a difficult offseason split between Tkachuk and the Senators. He spent eight seasons in Ottawa, serving as captain for five, before requesting a trade in 2026. The Senators eventually dealt him to the Panthers, where he joined his brother, Matthew.

Tkachuk appeared unfazed by the crowd's reaction and gave fans a smile during the tribute. He also opened the scoring, converting a power play to give Florida an early lead.

However, Ottawa soon responded through Tim Stützle before Claude Giroux and Shane Pinto helped the Senators build a commanding advantage. Warren Foegele and Stephen Halliday added third-period goals as Ottawa secured a 5-1 victory.

The game grew increasingly heated in the third period, with players from both teams involved in confrontations near Ottawa's bench. Brady Tkachuk also exchanged words with former teammate Dylan Cozens.

The loss ended Florida's three-game winning streak, while Ottawa improved to 7-3-0. Tkachuk's return became a memorable night, but not for the reasons he or the Panthers wanted.

For Senators fans, the tribute offered little reconciliation after the captain's departure. Their reaction showed how fast a celebrated relationship can turn bitter in professional hockey.

articles.body:
We are one day into the season, and already, the Golden State Warriors are seeking to make some changes on the trade market. Reports emerged on Wednesday that erstwhile starter Kristaps Porzingis is firmly on the trade block, and that the fragile center–who was re-signed on a two-year, $40 million contract but with only $2 million guaranteed for next year–could be had in a deal even though he has not been healthy enough to report to training camp and might be forced to retire.

The consensus around the league: The Warriors are a year late on this.

As ESPN's Shams Charania wrote on Twitter/X: "Porzingis is on a trade-flexible contract for $20 million this season and a small partial next year, serving as essentially an expiring deal that the Warriors can utilize, potentially with their pool of assets. He first revealed his POTS diagnosis last year and has had ups and downs with the issue. If there is no breakthrough in recovery, stepping away from basketball — for good — is possible."

Kristaps Porzingis Trade Would Need Sweeteners

Obviously, the first concern is for Porzingis's health. But if you're the Warriors, the next concern is who is going to start at center, and can they swap out Porzingis in a trade? Sure, but the challenge is putting together a deal that incentivizes another team to absorb Porzingis' $20 million, which would require the Warriors to take on money that goes beyond this season. More than that, it would require the Warriors to either give up a young player (they don't have many) or a first-round draft pick.

That would have been an attractive proposal … except the NBA changed the rules of the draft lottery a year ago and now, teams are not in the market to tank for fear of finishing in the bottom three and seeing their lottery odds take a hit.

One NBA executive said on Wednesday, "If they're taking back money and putting in a pick, that's great. But even the bad teams and the rebuilding teams are trying to win this year. It is going to be tough to get a team to give you a player you can use for one they can't use even if it gets you off a contract down the line."

There are possibilities for the Warriors. Maybe something could be worked out for, say, Myles Turner of the Bucks, or Daniel Gafford of the Mavericks or Nic Claxton of the Bulls. But again, those teams are not trying to tank, so there would be a risk in taking on Porzingis.

Also at stake: The Warriors' prized summer of 2027 cap space. Trading Porzingis and bringing in a player on a contract that has another $20 million-plus on it will take a sizable chunk out of the space the Warriors can anticipate next summer, from a bit more than $50 million to a bit more than $30 million.

"They can't just take a placeholder big guy if it is going to be someone who is there past this year," the exec said. "It's got to be someone you're building around, especially if you're giving up a pick. You're hurting yourself twice that way, once by giving up a pick, and once by cutting back on what you can do in free agency. It's kind of a tricky situation, they've got to get it right."

articles.title: ‘They’re Gonna Be a Play-In Team’ — NBA Champion Predicts Lakers Will Underperform Despite Boasting ‘One of the Best Offenses in the League’
articles.summary: The new-look Los Angeles Lakers feature an elite offensive unit led by their backcourt of Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves. Still, Kendrick Perkins has low expe...
articles.body:
The new-look Los Angeles Lakers feature an elite offensive unit led by their backcourt of Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves. Still, Kendrick Perkins has low expectations for how far they can go this season.

Perkins believes Dončić and Co. are destined to be a play-in team because of their defensive limitations.

Kendrick Perkins Predicts Lakers' Defense Will Hold Them Back

Now entering his ninth season, Dončić has proven time and again that he can lead a team offensively. He can create space, score from almost anywhere, and find his teammates with sharp, pinpoint passes.

Alongside him is Reaves, who is capable of scoring at all three levels. Even against tough defenses, he has shown that he can hit difficult shots and handle a complementary scoring role.

On paper, they should be one of the most difficult duos to contain this season.

Perkins, a member of the 2008 Boston Celtics title squad, believes in their offensive capabilities. However, he also doesn't think their offense will take them far, as he shared on "NBA Today" on Wednesday.

"Offensively, yes, Luka is one of the most offensive gifted players that we have ever seen in this game," Perkins said . "They have a lot of offensive talent. I believe they're going to be one of the best offensive teams in the league.

"I also believe that they're gonna be a play-in team because there's another side of the basketball. From what I've seen from Walker Kessler, from what I've seen from him in the preseason, he didn't show me that A-list center type energy."

Dončić does not seem slowed by defensive attention. He's already won two scoring titles, averaging 33.9 points per game in the 2023-24 campaign and 33.5 ppg last season. He also involves his teammates, averaging 8.2 assists per night over his first eight seasons.

Despite his offensive prowess, the six-time All-Star has been criticized for not having a strong defensive impact. The same can be said for Reaves, who lacks the skill set to be considered a good on-ball defender.

In an effort to address their defensive woes, the Lakers acquired Matisse Thybulle and Walker Kessler this past offseason.

Thybulle is a tremendous perimeter defender, capable of disrupting offenses and forcing turnovers. Through seven seasons, he's averaged 1.6 steals per game.

Kessler, meanwhile, combines his massive 7-foot-2 frame with excellent timing to protect the paint. He regularly blocks shots, averaging over 2 blocks per game in each of his first three campaigns. His fourth season was an exception, as he averaged just 1.8 blocks while being limited to five games due to a torn labrum in his left shoulder.

Still, Kessler and Thybulle can only do so much. The rest of the Lakers roster will also need to step up defensively. If they can improve on that end of the floor, Los Angeles could compete with the Western Conference's top teams for a shot at the title.

articles.title: Blake Griffin Is Pointing the Finger at the Wrong People in Sports Journalism
articles.summary: "If Griffin truly wants to champion sports journalism, his fight shouldn't be with the people entertaining audiences. It should be with the companies that de...
articles.body:
You have to love when people attempt to replicate success with a different spin on an established concept. The Daily Show has built a successful model around presenting news through satire, inspiring countless imitators. Now, Blake Griffin is trying his hand at the same concept, adding a sports twist.

With his new program, The Stepback with Blake Griffin , the former NBA top overall pick takes aim at sports headlines and topics through satire and commentary. The debut episode, published Tuesday evening, focused on the state of sports journalism in 2026. The content was well-written, delivered punchlines and identified its targets. Yet Griffin's argument missed a fundamental distinction: Much of what he criticized was exactly what those personalities, and now himself, deliver. Entertainment, not journalism.

Defining journalism has become increasingly difficult in today's media landscape. I've always viewed it as gathering facts, verifying information and presenting accurate stories independently of personal opinion. Audiences once had a clearer understanding of the difference between reporting and commentary. Those lines have blurred with the growth of columnists, radio, television, podcasting and digital media.

Today, facts and opinions are too often treated as interchangeable. That doesn't make them the same thing, nor does it make every personality discussing the news a journalist.

Griffin targeted familiar names, including Stephen A. Smith, Colin Cowherd and Skip Bayless. He criticized the embrace-debate model that helped propel First Take into the sports media stratosphere before networks across television copied the formula.

But embrace debate wasn't a new invention. Sports radio borrowed from the great columnists in every city, giving audiences not only the news of the day but also perspectives on what it meant. Reporting delivers the information. Commentary and reaction provide the entertainment.

Smith has a journalism background and continues to work sources for information. However, his presentation on First Take and his talk shows centers on opinion and debate. That's entertainment, not journalism. Their contributions can be valuable without being classified as traditional reporting.

No doubt, sports journalism doesn't look the way it once did. It hasn't for some time. However, Griffin attacking entertainers for failing to meet the standards of traditional journalism misses the larger issue.

Griffin is criticizing personalities for doing what their employers hired them to do.

Media needs a clearer distinction between journalism and entertainment. Dan Le Batard has argued that sports journalism is long dead, while his Meadowlark Media colleague Pablo Torre has established his own approach to investigative sports journalism. Regardless of where they stand, the industry needs to better explain the difference between informing an audience and engaging one.

Journalism presents verified information, facts and quotes, allowing audiences to draw their own conclusions. Entertainment uses information to frame opinions, reactions and personalities. Both have a place in sports media, but they serve different purposes.

"At some point, you have to ask yourself what exactly sports journalism on TV has been replaced with," Griffin said. "People with very little information and no expertise. Picking positions they don't actually believe in, and giving the hardest takes they can with zero accountability."

He's right that traditional sports journalism programming has changed. The Sports Reporters is no longer on television. Outside the Lines is now a podcast. SportsCenter once devoted its time to highlights, and lots of them.

But audiences and their expectations changed, forcing the industry to adapt. Accountability increasingly comes through viewership and engagement. Media companies either evolve with consumer habits or risk losing their audience.

"Maybe it's supposed to be entertainment. Maybe it's reality TV, or maybe it's pro wrestling kayfabe. But it's not reporting. It's a gimmick," Griffin said.

Again, agreed. It's not reporting, and therefore it isn't journalism. But the gimmick has found an audience and generated influence and advertising revenue, which is precisely what Griffin hopes to accomplish with his own program.

"The response of all these people might be, we're not saying we're journalists. But they're taking the desks, articles, and the airtime of journalists. They are journalism's replacement," Griffin said. "That matters because we need good sports journalism."

This is where Griffin's argument misses the mark entirely. Smith, Cowherd and Bayless didn't take seats away from quality journalists. Networks and publishers made business decisions about the content they wanted to produce and the personalities they wanted to feature.

Cowherd isn't on NPR. He's on FOX Sports Radio, a platform built around engaging personalities. Smith isn't presenting traditional reporting on ESPNews. He's on ESPN, where information, commentary, debate and entertainment coexist. Bayless now operates as a podcaster, sharing opinions on the day's headlines.

Griffin's frustration should be directed at the companies that prioritize those formats, not the people succeeding within them. Media is a business, and when the economics change, the product changes with them. That's why network television features fewer traditional sitcoms and more reality and game shows. The same economic pressures have transformed sports radio, while podcasting has drawn audiences toward niche programming, fewer commercial interruptions and on-demand content for a growing on-demand world.

Griffin is right to demand better sports journalism, more accountability and a clearer distinction between facts and opinions. But if he believes Smith, Cowherd and Bayless are responsible for its decline, he's pointing the finger in the wrong direction.

Those personalities didn't dismantle the business. They adapted to it.

The responsibility lies with the networks, publishers and media companies that decided personality-driven debate was a more profitable product than traditional reporting. They're the ones who determine what gets airtime, what gets funded and which voices audiences see and hear.

If Griffin truly wants to champion sports journalism, his fight shouldn't be with the people entertaining audiences. It should be with the companies that decided entertainment was the better business model in the first place. The problem isn't that sports media has too many personalities. It's that the industry increasingly prioritizes engagement over information, and no monologue aimed at the talent will fix that.

articles.title: Dale Steyn has a 3-word reaction to Harry Brook vs Marco Jansen 'best cricketer right now' debate
articles.summary: Former South African pace legend Dale Steyn has just three words to say about the debate raging on between Harry Brook and Marco Jansen for being the best cr...
articles.body:
South African legend Dale Steyn weighed in on a Harry Brook versus Marco Jansen debate with three words.

Nasser Hussain had called Brook the best cricketer in the world right now.

Steyn had made the same claim about Jansen a day later.

Dale Steyn doubles down in support of Marco Jansen as 'best cricketer' over Harry Brook

Dale Steyn needed only three words to make his case for Marco Jansen over Harry Brook after a fan put the two players side by side and asked which of them deserved to be called the best cricketer in the world right now.

The question arose because two respected voices had made competing claims within 24 hours of each other. Nasser Hussain had given the title to Brook, and Steyn had given it to Jansen the following day, which left supporters of both players arguing over who had the stronger claim.

One fan laid the contradiction out on X and invited people to pick a side. He wrote: "Yesterday – Nasser Hussain called Harry Brook the best cricketer right now. Today - Dale Steyn called Marco Jansen the best cricketer right now. - WHO DESERVES THE TITLE?"

Steyn saw the post and answered it himself, declining to make any sort of extended argument and instead offering a reply that ran to three words. He wrote , "Harry don't bowl."

Steyn believes Jansen's all-round value trumps Brook's batting

The logic behind the reply is straightforward enough. Brook is a specialist batter who does not bowl regularly, while Jansen is a genuine all-rounder who opens the bowling for South Africa and bats in the lower middle order, which means he contributes in two disciplines rather than one.

Steyn has long been an admirer, having worked closely with Jansen at Sunrisers Eastern Cape, and he has previously said the left-armer had not yet come close to realising his full potential.

At 2.06m, Jansen extracts bounce from almost any surface, and he is currently part of the South Africa squad facing Australia.

Brook's credentials are not in question either. He has spent much of the past two years at or near the top of the ICC Test batting rankings and has been England's most dependable batter across formats, which is why Hussain was willing to hand him the title in the first place.

Steyn's point is fair but it doesn't mean the debate is settled

There is something appealing about the brevity, and the underlying argument holds up. A cricketer who takes wickets and scores runs influences more of a match than one who only bats, and if the title is meant to recognise total contribution then an all-rounder of Jansen's standing will usually win that comparison.

The trouble is that "best cricketer" rarely means "most useful across disciplines" when people say it. Hussain was almost certainly talking about quality rather than breadth, and on that measure, Brook's batting record stands in comparison with anyone currently playing, Jansen included.

Both men are also being judged by people with a stake in the answer, which is worth remembering.

Steyn has mentored Jansen directly, and Hussain has watched Brook develop in the England setup, so neither verdict is quite the neutral assessment it might appear. The debate is fun, but it was never going to be settled in three words.

articles.title: Ashland sweeps Ontario, sets up district semi rematch with Columbian
articles.summary: It wasn't a perfect match by any means for Ashland, but it didn't have to be.
articles.body:
PHOTOS: #5 Ontario at #1 Ashland volleyball (Div. III sectional final)

ASHLAND - It wasn't a perfect match by any means for Ashland, but it didn't have to be.

After sweeping five-seed Ontario (5-18) in a Division III sectional championship 25-10, 25-16, 25-18, the top-seeded Arrows got exactly what they needed after more than a week off.

"I'm very happy to have this match to get tournament jitters out of the way before we move on to districts next week," coach Jenise Vaughn said. "It was a really good opportunity to get our kids in, and every single varsity player got to see the floor tonight. They deserved that, they work hard in practice every day."

Ashland's goal in the postseason opener was to start strong and storming out to an 8-1 lead forcing a timeout from Ontario coach Marlene Garber was about as perfect as Vaughn could've imagined.

"One of our goals was setting the tone and being the first to five points and I thought we played a tremendous game in set one," Vaughn said. "A lot of credit goes to Ontario, every team come tournament time is battling for their lives so you're going to see high emotions and teams that aren't going to give up ... they continued to battle, but I'm proud of how we closed this out in three."

The Warriors did make the Arrows fight in the second and third set staying within striking distance, but never got close enough to really make a charge at the end of either.

"We had an idea of what they were going to be like, we watched a lot of film and practiced based off of what their defense runs," Garber said. "Their defense is kind of similar to ours and we said — what's our weaknesses ... what can we build off of that and try to use that to our advantage with them? I think it definitely worked, they had some open spots we were able to hit at times, so I was proud of them."

Any time Ontario would start to make a run, the Arrows found a way to quash it and answer with a bigger run of their own. Sophomore Kyla O'Brien's hot hand serving in combination with Ashland's offensive depth made for a quick night with the match taking just over an hour.

"Her serves tonight were wicked, she was doing a great job of getting us on runs," Vaughn said of O'Brien, the Arrows finished with 11 aces. She's such a versatile player for us, so it was really exciting to see that come to fruition tonight.

"And I'm really happy with how our middle played tonight. Sadie Walter was an animal in the front row both blocking and hitting. And complementing her with Makenna Oslie and Ryland McFrederick on the outside, it's just hard to defense. I'm excited with how we can get multiple players involved in our offense."

While Ashland is moving on, Ontario's tumultuous fall comes to an end. The Warriors opened the season 2-1 with wins over rival Lexington and Clear Fork before going on a nine-game skid. Three wins in the next five matches against Galion, Northmor, and Harding were followed by six consecutive losses to close out including Wednesday's against the Arrows.

"Our team is very young, we really only have one running senior (Piper Studer) right now," Garber said. "With her gone we have three juniors coming up, four sophomores, and about 10 freshmen. Definitely a young team, but we're hoping over the next few years we can build and grow something that — maybe by the time our freshmen are seniors — we'll have something big.

"It has been good, it's just a long process."

And if anyone understands a long process, it's the Arrows. They went 4-20 just four years ago — right before this senior class entered high school — and they've trusted the process along the way to tying the single-season win record with 22 and winning the program's first Ohio Cardinal Conference title since 2017 .

Now they shift their sights to Monday's district semifinal (6 p.m.) against four-seed Tiffin Columbian, a team Ashland beat in four sets almost two months ago. But the Tornadoes have also won back-to-back district titles and are the team that has ended Ashland's tournament run each of the last two seasons.

"We had some success against them earlier this season, but when we've played them in the tournament in previous years, they've had the better results," Vaughn said. "We're excited to meet them again. They're a very dangerous team and they're very aggressive, so we'll practice that over the next few days and we'll be ready."

articles.title: Glenn Ordway Reveals Why He Came Out of Retirement To Launch ‘The Big O Podcast’
articles.summary: "I’ve been in the business for fifty years and have been around some great sports teams, memories and personalities. Why not just go back and reconnect with...
articles.body:
Retirement is both a blessing and a curse. It's a blessing because years of hard work and sacrifice allow a person to live life however they want after a certain point. It's a curse because finding ways to keep the days busy can be challenging. For Glenn Ordway , after nearly five decades in radio, it was time to retire from his role at Boston's WEEI four years ago. However, as time passed, his passion for sharing his thoughts with an audience re-emerged.

"The success I had in the [sports radio] business allowed me to live a pretty comfortable life. But to be honest, I just got bored [in retirement]," said Ordway. "It got to a point where you wake up on a Tuesday and ask, 'Do I want to play golf today?' Then you wake up Wednesday, and it's Groundhog Day with the same deal all over again. I needed something to do."

Just over a month ago, Ordway returned to the microphone. This time, he wasn't in Boston or even on terrestrial radio. Instead, he launched a podcast available in both audio and video formats on YouTube. The veteran Boston sports radio voice debuted The Big O Podcast , featuring stories, personalities and interviews from his legendary run at WEEI.

Although Ordway joked in his opening episode about being late to the podcasting party, the results have spoken for themselves. With more than 3,500 subscribers on YouTube alone and several episodes already released, Ordway has built a digital community rooted in storytelling. He's pulling back the curtain on some of Boston's biggest sports radio questions and most controversial moments.

"I've been in the business for fifty years and have been around some great sports teams, memories and personalities. Why not just go back and reconnect with all these moments and people?" explained Ordway. "But I was looking for what could get me the best kickstart out of the gate. There are so many unanswered questions regarding WEEI. I get those all the time. So, why not start with what happened with WEEI?"

The concept for The Big O Podcast began three years ago, after Ordway spent some time enjoying retirement through travel and time with family. However, two hip surgeries, including one that left him completely immobilized, forced him to delay the project several times.

After recovering, Ordway got healthy and lost a significant amount of weight. Eventually, he reached a point where he could begin the early stages of preparing the podcast for launch. Now, just over a month into the project, he says the response has been overwhelming. It has also created monetization opportunities he didn't have more than a decade ago during his first foray into podcasting.

"We've already been hit now by ad agencies that have contacted us with some opportunities. I heard that after the first week, which is amazing. I thought it would take at least six months," said Ordway. "Listeners want to go behind the curtain and know why certain things happened. Radio has trouble doing that because of sponsorships and people who could be affected by it."

Encouraged by the early success, Ordway has begun treating his podcast less like a side project and more like a business. He has plans to expand the operation immediately and into 2027.

"I'm into current sports. Now, I'm into college football because I have a lot of free time to watch it. So, we're going to do more sports stuff and spin it off into another channel," noted Ordway. "Also, two episodes per week will be [Boston] Celtics-related, featuring me, my son and a rotating third person from Celtics media or a former player. But I have other interests, too. In January, I hope to launch a podcast surrounding wine. The idea is to be a regular Joe who sells you on certain wines to try and enjoy."

Since retiring, Ordway has found himself consuming more podcasts than traditional sports radio. He listens not only to research best practices for commercial insertion and content development but also because he finds podcasts more relaxing and appreciates the room they give conversations to breathe.

Drawing from his research and enjoyment of several podcast categories, Ordway has taken a similar approach to The Big O Podcast that served him well for so many years at WEEI. He embraces an unfiltered style of discussion and storytelling that invites listeners into the personalities behind the content.

"I'm willing to talk about anything. In the business, there are certain things you just can't say that you want to. Back then, we were open about the behind-the-scenes aspects of the show and station because it was good fodder for the program," said Ordway. "I'm not taking anything to my grave."

As he revisits his days at WEEI, Ordway has held court with several of the station's current and former personalities, walking listeners down memory lane. He's sat down with Christian Fauria and Lou Merloni, as well as John Dennis, Kirk Minihane and Gerry Callahan. Those three separate conversations also led to an opportunity to reunite the popular Boston trio for an exclusive episode in the coming month.

Ordway maintains a list of potential guests, with each name accompanied by a page of stories he remembers. The notes help him prepare for each conversation. However, despite having a lengthy list of people he wants to interview, he recognizes that not everyone will agree to appear.

"I would love to have Rick Pitino on the program. Rick and I had a small conflict where I denied a request for him to appear on my show when he was at Boston University. Then, when he got the job with the Boston Celtics, good old Rick didn't forget that Ordway stiffed him back then," explained Ordway. "I don't want to just put people on that I've had great relationships with. I'd also like to put some on who I've had a terrible time with and reconcile before we find the eternal dirt nap. I'm trying to bring peace to the world."

Although Ordway still splits his time between his homes in Arizona and Boston, his perspective on Boston sports radio has evolved. He continues to listen to both major stations in the market, but he now follows their content primarily through social media clips rather than extended listening sessions.

For someone who was a giant of the format in Boston, Ordway has noticed significant changes in sports radio since stepping away.

"I made the mistake that a lot of others make when you're entrenched in it. When you have twenty hours of time to fill, you need to find every scab off a topic to extend it. Sometimes that can wear on an audience by trying too hard to find a negative," said Ordway. "No offense to anyone doing it. But in today's sports talk radio, there are more fake or pushed hot takes than ever before. There are people killing themselves to find a hot take, draw it out and throw it on the radio. But that's part of the business. It always has been."

Ordway sees a significant difference between hot-take radio and being unpredictable. He believes that sense of unpredictability is missing from today's sports radio landscape. He also says companies have changed how they define success. Whereas Nielsen ratings once served as the primary measuring stick, success now revolves more around protecting revenue and controlling expenses.

In retirement, Ordway says he doesn't have many regrets. However, he admits one of his biggest is failing to recognize the importance of building his own brand. It was an opportunity he didn't fully appreciate years ago.

"In 2009, when I was negotiating a new deal with WEEI, I had a group that came to me and offered me a deal to become my own brand. It was the group that put together the Dan Patrick Show," explained Ordway. "They wanted me to do a national show and a local show. But it was based on building my brand, not a radio station. If you have a pretty good brand already, spread it out now in digital media. Dan Patrick created a monster of a media operation. Best branding I've ever seen, and one of the greatest regrets of my life was not following Dan's lead. It was a huge mistake."

Ordway may regret passing up the opportunity to build his own brand nearly two decades ago, but he now has another chance to do so on his own terms. With decades of stories to tell, relationships to revisit and a growing audience eager to hear what happened behind the scenes at WEEI, The Big O Podcast has given him a renewed sense of purpose in retirement.

After nearly 50 years in radio, Ordway has learned that stepping away from the microphone doesn't necessarily mean walking away from the business.

"I'm getting back to my old roots, and I'm enjoying it immensely," said Ordway. "Hopefully that comes through to the audience willing to reconnect with an old friend."

Sometimes, all it takes is a little time away to rediscover what made you love something in the first place. If the early returns are any indication, the best chapters of Ordway's broadcasting career may still be ahead of him.

articles.title: Victor Wembanyama hopes to rediscover 'fun' after Thunder shut him down Opening Night
articles.summary: Victor Wembanyama hopes to rediscover 'fun' after Oklahoma City Thunder shut him down Opening Night.
articles.body:
Absolutely shocked at how things played out, Victor Wembanyama never reciprocated Chet Holmgren's Hulk-esque anger. For the first time in a while, the Oklahoma City Thunder got the absolute best of the San Antonio Spurs in a 116-104 win on Opening Night.

From the tipoff, Holmgren had it out for Wembanyama. He was glued to his lanky side on every possession. He rejected every chance to get a switch. Instead, last year's DPOY runner-up locked down the unanimous winner. To the tune of 12 points on an ugly 1-of-13 shooting.

It was quite the awakening for most of the NBA world. After last year's epic seven-game duel, most figured San Antonio had OKC's number. But this Opening Night win was the start of the Thunder erasing that national narrative and writing their own in favor of themselves.

Afterward, Wembanyama broke down what he did wrong against the team he sent home last year. The MVP candidate believes he must return to his dominant playing style. You can't keep relying on pull-up jumpers if you're 7-foot-4.

"I feel like it's obvious for me. I need to go back to playing the basketball I like. This is not the sport I like right here," Wembanyama said. "I got no reason to be hesitant, no reason to not be myself. For me, it's as simple as that. I'm good when I have fun."

Interesting to hear Wembanyama utter that sentiment. It's the first time in a minute that the Thunder bullied him out of his comfort zone. Usually, the Spurs have successfully spammed pick-and-roll lobs to their best player. But that option was completely sidelined.

That's something to watch for in future matchups. Did the Thunder crack the code at putting Holmgren on Wembanyama? Or will the Spurs make the proper adjustments? Don't expect another one-made field goal night from him. But perhaps OKC can force him into uncomfortable spots with its physically-branded defense.

It worked for one random October night, at least.

articles.summary: Both the Cardinal and Wolfpack have three wins, and they each need this to keep hope of a decent season alive. Here's the CFN game preview and prediction.
articles.body:
It's been a rocky ride for NC State. The team returned strong with hopes of being the ACC title mix, but everything all but ended in late August with a blowout loss to Virginia. A historically bad play against a lousy Vanderbilt team here, and a 38-14 home loss to a red-hot Wake Forest there, and now the Wolfpack need this. However, win, and there's a chance to go on a big second-half run with a favorable schedule. Stanford is trying to fight the good fight in a rebuild under new head coach Tavita Pritchard, but at 3-4 with only one home game left, it's in big trouble if it loses.

Why does Stanford need this? Three straight road games follow this, but that includes a trip up the road to Cal.

NC State only has one game – at Florida State – outside of North Carolina the rest of the way, hosting Cal, Duke, and Syracuse next.

The two programs have only met once. NC State beat Stanford 59-28 in 2024.

Date: Friday, October 23, 2026 Game Time: 10:30 PM ET TV: ESPN Location: Stanford Stadium, Palo Alto, CA – Week 8 Schedule & Predictions – What Will the CFP 12-Seed Bracket Be? – CFN Top 25 | Bowl Projections – CFN Expert Picks: Week 8

When Stanford's offense doesn't work, it really doesn't work. The lack of a pass rush and few defensive stops are the real issues, but you can't win if you don't score, and Stanford can't put the biscuit in the basket. Not to get all basic here, but the Cardinal have scored seven points or fewer in the four losses, and 34 or more in the three wins. The ground game has been non-existent against everyone but Elon and Hawaii. NC State is fantastic at keeping the chains moving. Stanford doesn't get to the quarterback and will struggle to hit Wolfpack star CJ Bailey enough to get off the field.

Okay, context time. Yeah, Stanford's offense was putrid in the four losses. One of those came against a nasty Duke defense Durham, and the other three losses were to Miami, Notre Dame, and a Wake Forest team whose only loss is to the Hurricanes. This is one of those focus-test moments for the ACC team from the Eastern Time Zone. This will end around 2 am NC State time, and while these are college kids who can certainly stay awake, the rhythm will be thrown off.

NC State vs Stanford Prediction, Betting Lines

Don't just blow this off as a layup win for NC State before getting back on the plane to go deal with bigger and better things. The Wolfpack have had to deal with a whole ton of adversity this season, and they keep coming back, but it's 0-2 on the road, and Stanford is 3-1 at home, with that one loss coming to Miami. NC State doesn't have the pass rush to overwhelm the Cardinal backfield, but it'll be just okay enough to get out with a tough late-night win.

articles.title: James Jones rushes for 178 yards and a touchdown as New Mexico State beats Sam Houston 30-24
articles.summary: HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — James Jones rushed for 178 yards and a touchdown, Adam Damante threw for two scores and New Mexico State beat Sam Houston 30-24 on W...
articles.body:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — James Jones rushed for 178 yards and a touchdown, Adam Damante threw for two scores and New Mexico State beat Sam Houston 30-24 on Wednesday night.

New Mexico State had touchdown drives of one and two plays in the second quarter to take a 14-10 lead into halftime. After Sam Houston State began the third with an 81-yard touchdown , the Aggies scored 16 straight points to go ahead 30-17.

Damante had a pass intercepted midway through the fourth and Sam Houston capitalized on the short field with a touchdown. But New Mexico State used six plays to go 44 yards and run out the clock.

Damante was 19 of 29 for 160 yards against one of the stingiest pass defenses in the country as Sam Houston entered allowing just 137.8 passing yards per game to rank fourth in the country. Only Texas Tech has eclipsed 200 yards passing against the Bearkats this season.

TJ Washington Jr. also had a rushing touchdown for New Mexico State (3-4, 2-1 Conference USA).

Landyn Locke threw for 235 yards with one touchdown and one interception for Sam Houston (1-6, 0-3). Locke, who entered with 11 touchdown passes averaging 34.5 yards for the second-highest average among FBS quarterbacks with at least 10 TD tosses this season, found Tim Burns Jr. over the middle on the first play of the third for the long touchdown.

Sam Houston took an early 7-0 lead after Terrence Guillory II blocked a punt and Sam Adams recovered it in the end zone for a touchdown.

New Mexico State: Returns home to play Jacksonville State on Oct. 28.

Sam Houston: Plays at Missouri State on Tuesday.

articles.title: Alabama Football Suffers Another Major Blow as Ryan Coleman-Williams Ruled Out Against Texas A&M
articles.summary: Sidelined with injury, the Crimson Tide’s leading receiver leaves a struggling offense searchng for rhythm and explosive plays against the Aggies’ aggressive...
articles.body:
Just when Alabama desperately needs its offense to find some consistency, the Crimson Tide has been dealt another significant blow.

Star wide receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams has officially been ruled out for Saturday's matchup against Texas A&M, marking the second consecutive game Alabama will be without one of its most explosive and reliable offensive weapons. Coleman-Williams , who also missed last weekend's disappointing 26-10 loss to Tennessee, remains sidelined as he recovers from injuries sustained earlier this season.

According to Wednesday's SEC availability report, Coleman-Williams will not suit up when Alabama welcomes the Aggies to Bryant-Denny Stadium for Homecoming. The news comes at a particularly difficult time for a Crimson Tide team searching for answers following back-to-back losses to Georgia and Tennessee.

And make no mistake about it: Alabama is going to miss him.

Through Alabama's first six games, Coleman-Williams established himself as one of the most important pieces of Ryan Grubb's offense. The junior recorded 23 receptions for 415 yards and four touchdowns, leading the Crimson Tide in all three categories.

But statistics alone don't tell the entire story of what Coleman-Williams brings to this football team.

His speed, explosiveness, route-running ability, and knack for creating separation have made him one of quarterback Keelon Russell's most dependable targets. Whether stretching the field vertically, creating explosive plays after the catch, or demanding attention from opposing defenses, Coleman-Williams provides an element that simply cannot be replicated overnight.

When a defense has to account for a receiver capable of changing the game with one touch, it opens opportunities for everyone else on the field. Without that threat, opposing defensive coordinators can become considerably more aggressive in how they attack Alabama's offense.

And unfortunately, we saw some of those challenges against Tennessee.

Alabama's offense struggled to establish rhythm, failed to consistently sustain drives, and committed four turnovers against the Volunteers. The Crimson Tide converted just two of its 13 third-down opportunities, another concerning statistic for an offense that has far too much talent to continue struggling at this level.

Coleman-Williams wouldn't have magically solved every offensive problem Alabama experienced in Knoxville, but his absence certainly didn't help.

With Coleman-Williams unavailable against Texas A&M, the responsibility falls on Alabama's remaining receivers to elevate their production.

Derek Meadows, Rico Scott, and Lotzeir Brooks will all be important pieces of the offensive game plan as Alabama attempts to rediscover the explosiveness that made this unit so dangerous earlier in the season.

Grubb acknowledged earlier this week that Meadows experienced the largest increase in playing time following Coleman-Williams' absence, while Scott and Brooks maintained workloads relatively similar to their previous roles.

But this weekend cannot simply be about replacing one player's production. It has to be about offensive execution across the board.

Russell must make better decisions with the football, Alabama's offensive line must provide more consistent protection, and Grubb must find creative ways to put his playmakers in favorable situations.

That means establishing offensive balance, utilizing formations that create mismatches, and making a concerted effort to get the football into the hands of players who can create explosive plays.

The question is whether the coaching staff can maximize that talent when one of its most important offensive weapons is standing on the sideline.

As frustrating as it is to lose Coleman-Williams for another important SEC matchup, his long-term health must remain the priority.

According to reports, the junior recently underwent arthroscopic knee surgery after dealing with a meniscus injury. He also suffered a concussion during Alabama's October 10 loss to Georgia. With the Crimson Tide scheduled for a bye week following Texas A&M, the additional recovery time could prove valuable.

Alabama travels to LSU on November 7, and getting Coleman-Williams healthy for the final stretch of the regular season would provide a tremendous boost to an offense desperately needing consistency.

Beyond his physical contributions, Alabama is missing one of its team captains and emotional leaders. Grubb specifically emphasized the positive influence Coleman-Williams has on his teammates, something that shouldn't be overlooked during a challenging stretch of the season.

At 5-2 overall and 3-2 in SEC play, Alabama is running out of opportunities to correct its mistakes and regain momentum. The loss of Coleman-Williams is significant, but it cannot become an excuse for another disappointing offensive performance.

Great football programs find ways to overcome adversity.

Great coaching staffs make adjustments when key players become unavailable.

And great teams refuse to allow injuries to determine the outcome of their seasons.

Saturday represents another opportunity for Alabama to prove it still belongs in the conversation among college football's best teams.

Coleman-Williams has already demonstrated how valuable he is to this offense. Now, with its leading receiver sidelined for a second consecutive week, the Crimson Tide must demonstrate something equally important.

That Alabama's success cannot depend on one player being healthy.

But potential doesn't win football games.

And against Texas A&M, Alabama absolutely must execute.

articles.title: Magic takeaways vs. Hawks: Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner, turnovers and more
articles.summary: Despite a 30-point double-double from Paolo Banchero, the Magic lost their regular-season opener on Wednesday, their first game under Sean Sweeney.
articles.body:
ORLANDO, Fla. -- Despite a 30-point double-double from Paolo Banchero, the Orlando Magic fell 132-125 to the Atlanta Hawks in their regular-season opener on Wednesday at the Kia Center, marking their first game under new coach Sean Sweeney.

Banchero finished with 35 points, 10 assists and seven rebounds, while Franz Wagner and Wendell Carter Jr. each scored 22 points and Desmond Bane added 18. Tristan da Silva led the Magic off the bench with 14 points, including four 3-pointers.

The Magic led by five after the first 12 minutes, but the Hawks held a 44-29 second-quarter lead to build a 10-point cushion at the break. Orlando responded by outscoring Atlanta 38-27 in the third quarter, including a 17-4 run that regained the lead.

The two teams traded the lead 22 times, including 11 in the fourth quarter. The Hawks stayed ahead for good behind clutch play from Nickeil Alexander-Walker, who scored 11 in the final period, including back-to-back 3s in the final two minutes.

Alexander-Walker led the Hawks with 31 points, Jalen Johnson recorded 20 points, 14 rebounds and six assists and Dyson Daniels had 20 points and five steals in their sixth straight win over the Magic. They outscored the Magic 60-50 in the paint and scored 24 points off 20 turnovers.

After falling to the Hawks, the Magic return Friday to host the Minnesota Timberwolves (1-0). The Hawks face the Charlotte Hornets (1-0) on the road Friday.

Here are five observations from the contest:

The Magic committed 13 turnovers in the first half, giving the Hawks 18 points. While they dished out 30 assists and had stellar ball movement at times, the group was affected by the Hawks' length and had several passes picked off or overdribbled into traffic. Several players were also whistled for moving screens.

The group settled down a bit in the second half, including only three turnovers in the third quarter, but its issues flared up again in the final frame at inopportune times. While they couldn't overcome their mistakes, the team believes it can correct them.

"That's the first game: We knew it wasn't going to be perfect," Carter said. "From some of the calls we were making in pick and rolls to some of the schemes we were running on the defensive end, for being out there and being in the mix, I feel like there are some things that we can definitely correct. I'm going to go back and watch the film, but I definitely feel like it is all correctable stuff. It is nothing that can't be fixed."

Said Banchero: "Continue to just build and watch the film tomorrow. I think it just starts with myself and the leaders on the team and really harping on the things that have been killing us and getting it cleaned up."

Banchero played like a former All-Star in a highly efficient contest, going 10-for-12 from the field, including 3-for-4 from 3-point range. He missed his first shot in the second quarter after knocking down his first five, and he wouldn't miss again until late in the third quarter.

The former Rookie of the Year also made 12-for-16 from the free-throw line, which he attributed to his ability to finish through contact at the rim. He was decisive in the paint and played methodically, which stood out to Carter after the game.

"When it is one move or no move, and he is just straight downhill, there are not many guys in this league who can guard him," Carter said. "Our style of play is to allow him to get into the paint quite easily and allow teammates to make decisions on the back end. ... If we continue to feed off him, and he continues to play the way he plays, we're going to be in a really good spot, for sure."

Wagner played just eight minutes in the first half after picking up three early fouls, recording seven points. He responded with 15 points in the second half, including 11 in the third quarter, which sparked their run to regain the lead.

With Wagner producing 22 points and Banchero scoring 35 points, it marked the 73rd time in their careers that they both had 20 or more in the same game. They received some offensive help from their teammates, but it is clear the Magic will likely go as far as Wagner and Banchero can take them.

After committing several turnovers and defensive lapses in the second quarter, the Magic responded after halftime with their best period of the evening. They managed to go on a run after Johnson was forced to sit after picking up his fourth foul.

They capitalized on the Hawks' foul trouble after getting into the bonus midway through the period, converting 15-for-20 from the charity stripe in the quarter alone. The group also rebounded well and turned the Hawks over six times in the period.

"I think (the third quarter) is one of the areas where we did a good job of sticking together and really putting our minds to what we need to do," Sweeney said. "Any time you see guys respond to something, that is great. Now we just need to do it better."

The Magic suffered several defensive lapses throughout the game, which is expected in the first game of the season under a new coach. They pointed to missed stops in key situations and letting shooters get open from the 3-point line, particularly in the fourth quarter.

The group will review the film and identify areas for improvement as it heads into its matchup against the Timberwolves on Friday. The team is confident it can fix those issues.

"There is plenty to work on, certainly," Sweeney said. "A lot of correctable things. Defensively, I think we can do a much better job than we did tonight, and we will do a much better job than we did tonight. Both sides of the ball, there is always things to improve upon."

articles.title: Bulls on wrong side of franchise history in opening loss vs. Raptors
articles.summary: The Chicago Bulls began the season with an aura of hope. That was largely due to the hype surrounding Caleb Wilson. However, Wednesday night showed that the...
articles.body:
The Chicago Bulls began the season with an aura of hope. That was largely due to the hype surrounding Caleb Wilson . However, Wednesday night showed that the youngsters are experiencing real growing pains.

The Bulls lost their season opener on the road to the Toronto Raptors by 43 points, 135-92. In the process, they suffered the biggest season-opener defeat in franchise history, per K.C. Johnson of Chicago Sports Network. The previous mark was by 25 points in 2001 and 2003.

The Bulls showed a wide range of vulnerabilities that often come with opening-game jitters, especially for a young, rebuilding team. For starters, Chicago committed 27 total turnovers, including 11 in the first half alone. Caleb Wilson finished with 9 turnovers and Josh Giddey with 5.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

In addition, Josh Giddey was overwhelmed by the posterizing Toronto defense. Plus, Chicago didn't have anyone on the floor who was close to 7 feet tall. After all, Nic Claxton remains out with a hamstring injury sustained in a preseason practice.

Also, even though Caleb Wilson got his first dunk , he shot 1-for-8 from the 3-point line and 7-for-21 from the field. Altogether, he finished with 16 points and 4 rebounds.

Matas Buzelis led the way with 17 points, including going 13-for-16 from the free-throw line. Also, Jalen Smith, filling in for Claxton in the paint, finished with 15 points and 8 rebounds. Norman Powell scored 15 points in his Bulls debut. Tre Jones finished with 13 points.

Josh Giddey only finished with 2 points, going 1-for-10 from the field. He finished with 7 rebounds and 6 assists.

On Friday, the Bulls will head to Milwaukee to play the Bucks in a rescheduled game due to Game 1 of the World Series. The next day, Chicago will play their home opener against the Washington Wizards.

articles.title: Giannis Antetokounmpo takes accountability for the Heat's loss in the season opener
articles.summary: The Heat lost their first game of the season, and Giannis Antetokounmpo is shouldering the blame.
articles.body:
In the 2026 offseason, the Miami Heat made a big addition by trading for Giannis Antetokounmpo. They added a superstar to a good team, which has made them one of the favorites in the Eastern Conference.

They had a good preseason, but they started the 2026-27 season with a loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves . As the star player, Giannis has taken accountability for the loss, as he wants to set the tone for the team.

Giannis Antetokounmpo shoulders the blame for the Heat losing their first game

It was a bad game for the Heat as they lost in a blowout, 131-106. The Timberwolves utterly dominated the game, as Anthony Edwards dominated with 45 points and 10 rebounds. LaMelo Ball supported him with 21 points of his own.

For the Heat, Giannis delivered because he had a 35-point performance. However, the rest of the team struggled to contain the Timberwolves' firepower.

As the superstar and one of the Heat's leaders, Antetokounmpo has personally taken on the responsibility for the loss. He does not want to see it happen again, which is why he's making sure to speak on the issues from the first loss.

"Our effort gotta be way better. It starts with me; my effort gotta be better. Our effort was not as good as it was in the past. I have to be better; it starts with me. I have to set the tone," Antetokounmpo said after the season opener loss .

With the team's struggles being apparent, Giannis wants to resolve it as soon as possible. The Heat want to compete for the championship, so if they manage to take care of these issues, they will be golden.

articles.title: Takeaways for UCLA's 100-53 exhibition win over California Baptist
articles.summary: UCLA basketball impressed with a 100-53 win over California Baptist on Wednesday. Eric Dailey Jr. led the team with 25 points.
articles.body:
It was quite the debut for the 2026-2027 UCLA Bruins men's basketball team, with the season getting underway with an exhibition game against California Baptist on Wednesday. UCLA picked up a 100-53 win in a dominant showing for Mick Cronin's team .

For UCLA to compete at the top of the Big Ten Conference, the team will need some returners to take the next step. One of those returners is Eric Dailey Jr. , who played perhaps his best game as a Bruin. Dailey scored 25 points while hitting seven of his nine three point attempts.

Serbian freshman Nikola Kusturica lived up to the hype too, scoring 10 points but showcasing his all-around game. Kusturica added eight rebounds, six assists with five steals and two blocks. If Kusturica doesn't have to immediately take on the burden of the team's primary scorer, he will excel as UCLA's 17-year old jack-of-all-trades.

Cronin went for a starting lineup of Dailey and Kusturica at the forward positions, with Trent Perry and Jalen Petty in the backcourt with Xavier Booker at center. That's a talented starting lineup, loaded with scoring options and provides defensive versatility on the backend.

Plenty of intensity for the exhibition game

The game was against California Baptist but UCLA's effort was on full display. The team brought down 57 rebounds and were in passing lanes all night, leading to countless steals for the UCLA defense.

Joe Philon impressed off the bench too, slamming home a big breakaway dunk and playing with high intensity for a freshman getting his first taste of college basketball.

UCLA will hope to have plenty of more important wins this season but Wednesday was a good beginning for this year's Bruin squad.
